newsitem.title: MEXICO: Archaeologists survive Mexico jungle machete attack.
newsitem.headline: Archaeologists survive Mexico jungle machete attack.

text.p: A leading Australian archaeologist and his expedition have emerged alive from Mexico's southeastern rainforest after being attacked by machete-wielding Indians, his associates said on Tuesday.

Australian Peter Matthews and other members of the 12-strong expedition were ambushed on Friday by up to 80 Mayan Indians armed with machetes, sticks and firearms, said Carlos Silva Rhoads, director of the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) in southeastern Chiapas state.

One man, badly beaten and his face slashed by a machete, fled following the assault and made an 80-mile (130 km) trek northwest through the jungle to the world-famous archaeological ruins and town of Palenque, one report said.

Matthews, the expedition leader, and his Mexican colleague Nazario Totosahur reportedly threw themselves into a roaring jungle river to escape the attack that took place near the village of El Cayo, close to the Guatemalan border.
The rest of the group was released after being kidnapped and robbed by Indians trying to prevent them from removing a 1,300-year-old Mayan altar.
"The Indians held them for three days. They were freed one by one over the course of yesterday (Monday)," said Mauricio Avila, an INAH official in Mexico City.

"The Indians wanted to defend the altar with violence," Silva said in a telephone interview from Chiapas state. "But they were not only trying to defend the nation's heritage. They also wanted money."

The expedition had permission both from the Mexican authorities and from local villagers to bring the altar to a specially built auditorium in the town of Frontera Corrozal for protection, Silva said.
